# jev-opt hint search --- state format state-v4.1-2026-09-22, vocabulary v4-2026-09-22

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

target        hintbench
binary        hintbench
toolchain     rustc 1.100.0-nightly (bba531001), LLVM 23.1.1
machine       AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512), one physical core
recipe        -Copt-level=3, fat LTO, 1 codegen unit, -Cdebuginfo=1,
              -Ctarget-cpu=native, PGO (-Cprofile-use, one shared profile),
              -Cllvm-args=-hints-allow-reordering=false
measurement   8 case(s): k1, k2, k3, k4, k5, k6, k7, k8
              15 interleaved repetitions, shuffled label order, paired
              bootstrap 95% CI, speed ratio = baseline time / this build's time
              (greater than 1 is faster)
source        source_comments: strip --- every comment and doc attribute is
              removed from the source excerpts below before they are
              quoted, and a line that held nothing else is shown as
              `// [comment removed]`. Line numbers are the file's
              own and are unchanged.

## The machine this will run on

  cpu model         AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core Processor, 16 core(s) / 32 logical cpu(s), family 25 model 33
  llvm target-cpu   znver3 (what -Ctarget-cpu=native resolves to on this machine)
  isa               avx2, avx, fma, bmi1, bmi2, aes, sha_ni, vaes, vpclmulqdq, popcnt, movbe, rdseed, adx, clwb, clflushopt, erms, fsrm, sse4_2
  no isa            **no AVX-512 of any kind**
  vector width      256 bit, 16 architectural vector registers
                    one register holds 32 x u8, 16 x u16, 8 x u32/f32, 4 x u64/f64
  l1 data           32 KiB, 8-way, shared by cpus 0-1
  l1 instruction    32 KiB, 8-way, shared by cpus 0-1
  l2 unified        512 KiB, 8-way, shared by cpus 0-1
  l3 unified        32 MiB, 16-way, shared by cpus 0-31
  how it is read    lscpu and /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache on this machine, once per run. This is a WSL2 guest: the cache figures are the guest-visible ones and are reported as seen, not corrected.
  how it is timed   the process is pinned to one logical cpu (taskset -c 8) with a 0 ms settle gap between runs, 15 interleaved repetitions, shuffled label order, paired bootstrap 95% CI

## Where the hints are applied

Function attributes are applied at PipelineStartEP, before any inlining.
Loop metadata is applied at VectorizerStartEP, after inlining and loop
canonicalisation and immediately before LoopVectorize, so a loop hint acts on
the loop as it exists after the function attributes of this same round have
already taken effect.

  hbkernels::k1_step                                            profile share 12.50%, 0 loop site(s)
  hbkernels::k2_mix                                             profile share 12.50%, 0 loop site(s)

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## Where the hints are applied

Function attributes are applied at PipelineStartEP, before any inlining.
Loop metadata is applied at VectorizerStartEP, after inlining and loop
canonicalisation and immediately before LoopVectorize, so a loop hint acts on
the loop as it exists after the function attributes of this same round have
already taken effect.

to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

Loop metadata is applied at VectorizerStartEP, after inlining and loop

q0.instructions:
Section `q0` of the state describes one loop inside a marked function of this program. Which single hint from the list is most likely to make this loop faster on this workload?

Mechanical readings for this site. Each line is produced by a tool from the numbers and the compiler remarks already in the state, by the same rule at every site in this request; none of them is an opinion about which hint to choose.
  - average trip count: 4096.0; trip class long (rule: <2 degenerate, <16 short, <100 medium, >=100 long)
  - body size: 8 LLVM instructions; size class tiny (rule: <50 tiny, <300 small, <1000 medium, <2000 large, >=2000 very large)
  - calls inside the body: no; loop nesting depth 2; loops this site key names: not recorded for this key (a key can name several loops, and a hint on it would reach all of them)
  - element type at the loop's iterator: u32 (read off the inline chain); one 256-bit vector register holds 8 of them, so the widest `vectorize.width` in this list that fits one register is 8 (the list stops at 16)
  - from the plugin's dump, which is the primary source here because it records this loop and not a source line: trip count 4096.0, calls in the body no, `llvm.loop.isvectorized` metadata at the point the hint is attached: no --- the hint goes in before LoopVectorize runs, so `no` is the normal reading and says nothing about whether LLVM vectorises this loop afterwards
  - vectorisation legality: UNKNOWN (shared source line; remarks not attributable to this loop) --- macros.rs:180 carries 17 separate vectoriser verdicts in the baseline build, because every loop inlined from that line lands on it. Nothing in the remarks can be read as a statement about this loop.
  - caveat that applies to every loop here: remarks carry a source location and no function name, so a line several inlined loops share carries all of their remarks at once; the readings above use this loop's own leaf location only, and say UNKNOWN where that location is shared

criteria.KEEP_DEFAULT: Attach no metadata to this loop. This is the 'no change' option: LLVM's vectoriser and unroller decide with their own cost model, exactly as in the baseline.
criteria.unroll_count_2: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.count = 2`: unroll the loop body twice. Halves the loop-control overhead and gives the scheduler two iterations to interleave. Note that this runs after vectorisation, so on a loop LLVM vectorises it unrolls the *vector* loop.
criteria.unroll_count_4: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.count = 4`: unroll the loop body four times. More scheduling freedom and fewer branches than count=2, at four times the body's code size and a longer remainder loop.
criteria.unroll_count_8: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.count = 8`: unroll the loop body eight times. Only worth it for a very short body with a high trip count; otherwise the code growth costs more in instruction cache than the saved branches are worth.
criteria.unroll_disable: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.disable`: forbid unrolling this loop entirely. Keeps the body small, which helps when the loop is short and unpredictable or when the caller's instruction footprint is the problem.
criteria.vectorize_width_2: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 2` (and `vectorize.enable`): force two lanes per vector iteration. ## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

binary        hintbench
toolchain     rustc 1.100.0-nightly (bba531001), LLVM 23.1.1

recipe        -Copt-level=3, fat LTO, 1 codegen unit, -Cdebuginfo=1,
              -Ctarget-cpu=native, PGO (-Cprofile-use, one shared profile),
              -Cllvm-args=-hints-allow-reordering=false
measurement   8 case(s): k1, k2, k3, k4, k5, k6, k7, k8

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

target        hintbench
binary        hintbench
toolchain     rustc 1.100.0-nightly (bba531001), LLVM 23.1.1
machine       AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512), one physical core
recipe        -Copt-level=3, fat LTO, 1 codegen unit, -Cdebuginfo=1,
              -Ctarget-cpu=native, PGO (-Cprofile-use, one shared profile),
              -Cllvm-args=-hints-allow-reordering=false
measurement   8 case(s): k1, k2, k3, k4, k5, k6, k7, k8

              bootstrap 95% CI, speed ratio = baseline time / this build's time

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

target        hintbench
binary        hintbench
toolchain     rustc 1.100.0-nightly (bba531001), LLVM 23.1.1
machine       AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512), one physical core
recipe        -Copt-level=3, fat LTO, 1 codegen unit, -Cdebuginfo=1,
              -Ctarget-cpu=native, PGO (-Cprofile-use, one shared profile),
              -Cllvm-args=-hints-allow-reordering=false
measurement   8 case(s): k1, k2, k3, k4, k5, k6, k7, k8

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

binary        hintbench
toolchain     rustc 1.100.0-nightly (bba531001), LLVM 23.1.1

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## The build every arm shares

criteria.vectorize_width_8: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 8` (and `vectorize.enable`): eight lanes per vector iteration. For 32-bit elements that is one 256-bit register; for 64-bit elements it is two, which LLVM will split.
criteria.vectorize_width_16: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 16` (and `vectorize.enable`): sixteen lanes per vector iteration. Only 8-bit and 16-bit element types fit that in one AVX2 register; for anything wider LLVM emits several registers per iteration, which can pay off on a very long loop and hurts on a short one.
criteria.interleave_count_1: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 1`: vectorise without interleaving, i.e. one vector body per iteration and a single accumulator chain. Shortens the loop and the remainder when LLVM's default interleaving was too aggressive.

criteria.interleave_count_4: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 4`: four independent vector chains per iteration. The most latency hiding of the three and the most register pressure; on a short trip count the remainder loop eats the gain.

criteria.unroll_disable: Attach `llvm.loop.unroll.disable`: forbid unrolling this loop entirely. Keeps the body small, which helps when the loop is short and unpredictable or when the caller's instruction footprint is the problem.
criteria.vectorize_width_2: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 2` (and `vectorize.enable`): force two lanes per vector iteration. A narrow forced width is a way to keep vectorisation but cut the cost of the scalar remainder when the trip count is low. Reassociation of floating-point reductions stays forbidden (the build pins -hints-allow-reordering=false), so a non-reassociable reduction will simply not be widened.
criteria.vectorize_width_4: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 4` (and `vectorize.enable`): four lanes per vector iteration. On this machine (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512) that is one 256-bit register for 64-bit elements.
criteria.vectorize_width_8: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 8` (and `vectorize.enable`): eight lanes per vector iteration. For 32-bit elements that is one 256-bit register; for 64-bit elements it is two, which LLVM will split.
criteria.vectorize_width_16: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 16` (and `vectorize.enable`): sixteen lanes per vector iteration. Only 8-bit and 16-bit element types fit that in one AVX2 register; for anything wider LLVM emits several registers per iteration, which can pay off on a very long loop and hurts on a short one.
criteria.interleave_count_1: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 1`: vectorise without interleaving, i.e. one vector body per iteration and a single accumulator chain. Shortens the loop and the remainder when LLVM's default interleaving was too aggressive.
criteria.interleave_count_2: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 2`: two independent vector chains per iteration, which hides the latency of a dependent reduction at the cost of more registers.
criteria.interleave_count_4: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 4`: four independent vector chains per iteration. The most latency hiding of the three and the most register pressure; on a short trip count the remainder loop eats the gain.

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

criteria.interleave_count_4: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 4`: four independent vector chains per iteration. The most latency hiding of the three and the most register pressure; on a short trip count the remainder loop eats the gain.

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

## What is being decided

A Rust program is compiled with one frozen recipe. The only thing that varies
between builds is a set of optimisation hints attached to named functions and
to the loops inside them; no source file is ever edited. You are shown one
site per question and you choose one hint for it from a fixed list. All the
questions in this request are answered independently and they all take effect
in the same build, which is then measured as a whole.

One of the options at every site is "no change", which reproduces the
baseline at that site. It is one option among the others, neither preferred
nor discouraged. The measurement is end-to-end wall time over the case set
below; the noise floor of this machine is about 1% aggregated. Hints that
change the program's output are rejected regardless of speed.

criteria.vectorize_width_2: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 2` (and `vectorize.enable`): force two lanes per vector iteration. A narrow forced width is a way to keep vectorisation but cut the cost of the scalar remainder when the trip count is low. Reassociation of floating-point reductions stays forbidden (the build pins -hints-allow-reordering=false), so a non-reassociable reduction will simply not be widened.
criteria.vectorize_width_4: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 4` (and `vectorize.enable`): four lanes per vector iteration. On this machine (znver3, AVX2, no AVX-512) that is one 256-bit register for 64-bit elements.
criteria.vectorize_width_8: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 8` (and `vectorize.enable`): eight lanes per vector iteration. For 32-bit elements that is one 256-bit register; for 64-bit elements it is two, which LLVM will split.
criteria.vectorize_width_16: Attach `llvm.loop.vectorize.width = 16` (and `vectorize.enable`): sixteen lanes per vector iteration. Only 8-bit and 16-bit element types fit that in one AVX2 register; for anything wider LLVM emits several registers per iteration, which can pay off on a very long loop and hurts on a short one.
criteria.interleave_count_1: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 1`: vectorise without interleaving, i.e. one vector body per iteration and a single accumulator chain. Shortens the loop and the remainder when LLVM's default interleaving was too aggressive.
criteria.interleave_count_2: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 2`: two independent vector chains per iteration, which hides the latency of a dependent reduction at the cost of more registers.
criteria.interleave_count_4: Attach `llvm.loop.interleave.count = 4`: four independent vector chains per iteration. The most latency hiding of the three and the most register pressure; on a short trip count the remainder loop eats the gain.
